recentItems.title: Trump administration plans to install signs warning of 'ideological bias' at a Smithsonian Museum
recentItems.description:
The Trump Administration is preparing to install signs in Washington, D.C., that warn against “ideological bias” at the Smithsonian.

The Interior Department says the signs will comply with President Trump’s July executive order, called “Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution.” In a Sept. 3 letter to Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the signs would warn visitors that the National Museum of American History is being used "as a tool to advance personal, radical ideologies." The 12 signs cost an estimated $7,000 each.

recentItems.title: Dolly Parton corn mazes open across the U.S. and Canada
recentItems.description:
Several corn mazes are cropping up across the country that are designed to look like Dolly Parton’s face.

The theme was chosen back in May — before the iconic country singer’s death last month. Organizers say they’re using the mazes to raise money for Parton’s literacy program, the Imagination Library. The program has provided more than 300 million books to children around the world and was a tribute to Parton’s father, who couldn't read or write.

recentItems.title: Trump administration takes aim at endangered species, again
recentItems.description:
A new internal memo from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service targets the Endangered Species Act — by reconsidering the word “take.”⁠
⁠
“Take” has long referred to both the intentional and accidental injury or killing of an endangered species. The memo suggests the government would do away with the accidental element. In a statement to NPR, the U.S. Department of the Interior wrote, “‘take’ continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife.”⁠
⁠
Environmental groups say they plan to sue.⁠
⁠

recentItems.title: Trump renews his threats to demolish the Kennedy Center
recentItems.description:
The Kennedy Center has been temporarily closed as President Trump renewed his threats this week to demolish the performing arts center.

Trump and his handpicked board of directors tried to put his name on the building, but a judge ordered it removed. Trump has threatened to demolish the building if his name isn't on it, arguing that, for his involvement in running and preserving the center, "I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition." Wednesday night, a news photographer took a picture of Trump on Air Force One in which the president is looking at a large placard that refers to the center having been demolished.

The status of the center has been the subject of a blizzard of emergency filings in federal court. Judge Christopher Cooper ruled Thursday the Trump administration must give 30 days' notice before taking any physical action on the building.

recentItems.title: Fuel prices continue to rise as Houthis block Saudi oil exports
recentItems.description:
Gas and diesel prices continue to soar.

AAA says the price of regular gasoline rose another seven cents overnight, to nearly $4.44 a gallon — a price that's never been higher this late in the year. Diesel, meanwhile, hit another all-time high today, too, jumping nearly nine cents overnight, to nearly $6.40 a gallon.

The conflict in Iran is forcing up prices, but Saudi Arabia’s oil exports have been slashed recently, too, because of its renewed war with the Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.

recentItems.title: Turkey rounds up LGBTQ Turks, it says, to protect Turkish families
recentItems.description:
Dozens of demonstrators are under arrest in Turkey after protesting the detention of LGBTQ+ activists in weekend raids. The government says it’s protecting Turkish families.⁠
⁠
The Turkish government is acting under the "My Family is Safe" initiative, framing the arrests as a defense of traditional family values. Turkish authorities broke into popular LGBTQ+ hangouts and raided activists’ offices across the country on Sunday. Homosexuality is not illegal in Turkey, but President Erdogan has called the LGBTQ+ community "deviants" to appeal to his conservative base.⁠
⁠

recentItems.title: Why are doomed beach homes left fully furnished?
recentItems.description:
Dramatic videos show waterfront houses collapsing into the water. It’s happening across the United States, from California to Michigan to Maine. 

One hotspot is Dare County, N.C., where more than 30 homes have collapsed since 2020, including one as recently as this summer. About 100 additional houses there are threatened by erosion exacerbated by sea level rise.

Yet there is no plan to remove most of the threatened houses — or to empty them of personal belongings before they fall — because of perverse incentives created by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). 

NPR dug into the upside-down world of FEMA flood insurance in coastal areas, and found many homeowners have no financial choice but to let their homes collapse. That’s leading to massive amounts of debris and pollution, which closes beaches, threatens wildlife and necessitates costly taxpayer-funded cleanup efforts.

And the problem is only getting worse. As climate-driven sea level rise accelerates erosion around the country, there is growing alarm among waterfront homeowners, local officials and even members of Congress. Everyone agrees the status quo is unsustainable. But can they agree on a long-term solution?

recentItems.title: Multistory building damaged by Israeli bombardments collapses in Gaza overnight
recentItems.description:
Authorities in Gaza say at least 20 people have been killed after a multistory building collapsed overnight. The U.N. humanitarian office says about 100 people were sheltering there — about half of them children. The building had been damaged earlier by Israeli bombardment. More people are still missing.

U.N. aid agencies are urging Israel to approve the entry of heavy machinery to Gaza to help lift rubble. They’re also asking for more tents and basic supplies for people, ahead of winter storms.

recentItems.title: Famed fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie dies at 87
recentItems.description:
Famed costume designer Bob Mackie died Monday. He was 87 years old.

Mackie was known as the “Sultan of Sequins” for the show-stopping looks he created for famous performers, and his dazzling designs became as memorable as the stars who wore them — think Cher's feathered mohawk headdress at the 1986 Oscars. He designed an estimated 17,000 costumes for Carol Burnett's variety show, including a famous dress made out of a pair of curtains from her 1976 "Gone with the Wind" parody.

Mackie won nine Emmy Awards and a Tony Award and continued dressing stars into the 21st century like Miley Cyrus and Pink.

Host: Korva Coleman/NPR
Reporter: Chloe Veltman/NPR

recentItems.title: Apple TV's 'Widow's Bay' wins big with 14 Emmy Awards
recentItems.description:
There was a big winner during last night’s Emmy Awards for the best in television: The horror comedy "Widow’s Bay" picked up 14 trophies.

Matthew Rhys was crowned best lead actor in a comedy for his role as the mayor of Widow’s Bay, a haunted New England island. His costars Kate O’Flynn and Stephen Root both won supporting actor awards. Rhys also made history by winning two lead actor Emmys at the same ceremony — the Welsh actor also won for his role in the series "The Beast in Me."

Jean Smart also picked up her fifth Emmy Award in a row for best comedy actress in the show "Hacks." The best male dramatic actor was Noah Wyle for his star role in the show "The Pitt." The best variety show winner was the "Late Show with Stephen Colbert," which was canceled by CBS earlier this year.
